cards.definition: A part of speech is the job a word does in a sentence, like naming or doing.
cards.explanation: A word class: a group of words that behave the same way in grammar. The main English word classes are noun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, determiner, pronoun and conjunction (interjection is often added).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The dog ran fast. The marked part “dog” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A noun names a person, animal, place, thing, idea or feeling.
cards.explanation: A word that names a person, place, thing, idea or quality. Nouns can usually follow a determiner such as the (“the ___ matters”) and can be singular or plural.
cards.illustrationAlt: A golden dog stands beside a red ball in a park.

cards.definition: A common noun names any person, place or thing, not one special one.
cards.explanation: A noun that names a general class of people, places or things (girl, city, river). It is not capitalized unless it starts a sentence.
cards.illustrationAlt: Three different dogs sit together with blank collar tags.

cards.definition: A proper noun is the special name of one person, place or thing. It starts with a capital letter.
cards.explanation: A noun that names a particular person, place, day, organization or thing (Maya, Texas, Monday) and is written with a capital letter.
cards.illustrationAlt: One golden puppy wears a large blank name tag; accompanying text supplies the name Rex.

cards.definition: A concrete noun names something you can see, touch, hear, smell or taste.
cards.explanation: A noun that refers to a physical thing that can be perceived with the senses (apple, drum, rain).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The apple fell. The marked part “apple” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: An abstract noun names an idea or feeling you can’t touch, like love or bravery.
cards.explanation: A noun that names an idea, quality, state or feeling rather than a physical object (childhood, courage, freedom).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Her courage helped us. The marked part “courage” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A collective noun names a group as one thing, like a team or a flock.
cards.explanation: A noun that names a group of people, animals or things as a single unit (team, flock, class, herd).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: A flock of birds landed. The marked part “flock” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A countable noun names things you can count: one cookie, two cookies.
cards.explanation: A noun with singular and plural forms that can be counted with numbers and used with a/an and many/few (a book, three books).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: We packed three cookies. The marked part “cookies” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: An uncountable noun names stuff you can’t count one by one, like water or sand.
cards.explanation: A noun that usually has no plural and is used with words like much, little or some (water, money, rice, air).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Please add some water. The marked part “water” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A possessive noun shows who owns something, using ’s, like the dog’s bone.
cards.explanation: A noun form, usually made with an apostrophe (’s or s’), that shows ownership or a close relationship (the girl’s book, the boys’ team).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Sam’s kite flew. The marked part “Sam’s” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: Singular means just one.
cards.explanation: The form of a noun, pronoun or verb used for one person or thing (cat, she, runs).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: One cat sleeps. The marked part “cat” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A plural noun means more than one, like cats or boxes.
cards.explanation: A noun form showing more than one, usually made by adding -s or -es (dogs, wishes).
cards.illustrationAlt: Three orange cats sit in a row.

cards.definition: An irregular plural changes in a special way, like mouse to mice.
cards.explanation: A plural that is not formed by adding -s or -es (feet, children, teeth, mice, fish).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Two mice hid. The marked part “mice” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A pronoun takes the place of a noun, like he, she, it or they.
cards.explanation: A word used in place of a noun or noun phrase (I, you, she, it, they, this, who). Pronouns let writers avoid repeating nouns.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Mia smiled because she won. The marked part “she” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: Personal pronouns stand for people or things: I, you, he, she, it, we, they.
cards.explanation: Pronouns that refer to specific people or things and change form for person, number and case (I/me, she/her, they/them).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: We waved at Sam. The marked part “We” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A possessive pronoun shows ownership and stands alone: mine, yours, his, hers, ours or theirs.
cards.explanation: A possessive pronoun stands in for a noun phrase and expresses ownership or another relationship: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs. Before a noun, my, your, her, our and their are possessive determiners. Some school grammars group both sets as possessive pronouns.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: That kite is mine. The marked part “mine” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A reflexive pronoun points back to the subject: myself, yourself, themselves.
cards.explanation: A pronoun ending in -self or -selves that refers back to the subject of the same clause (I hurt myself).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The cat washed itself. The marked part “itself” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: An intensive pronoun adds extra push, like “I made it myself!”
cards.explanation: A -self or -selves pronoun used to emphasize a noun or pronoun. It can appear beside the noun or later in the clause: The coach herself cheered; I made it myself. Removing it leaves the basic meaning intact.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The chef himself served us. The marked part “himself” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A relative pronoun like who, which or that starts a clause that tells more about a noun.
cards.explanation: A pronoun (who, whom, whose, which, that) that begins a relative clause and refers back to a noun in the main clause.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The boy who lives here waved. The marked part “who” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: Demonstratives point to things: this, that, these and those.
cards.explanation: Words that point out which one: this/these (near) and that/those (far). Used before a noun they are determiners; used alone they are pronouns.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Those apples are ripe. The marked part “Those” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: An indefinite pronoun refers to people or things without naming exactly which ones: someone, everyone or anything.
cards.explanation: A pronoun that refers to people or things in general rather than specific ones (anyone, everything, somebody, none, each).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Someone knocked. The marked part “Someone” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: Question words ask: who, what, where, when, why and how.
cards.explanation: Words used to ask questions (who, what, which, whose, where, when, why, how). Who, what, which and whose can act as interrogative pronouns.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Who ate the sandwich? The marked part “Who” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: The antecedent is the noun a pronoun points back to.
cards.explanation: The noun or noun phrase that a pronoun refers to and stands in for. Pronouns should agree with and clearly point to their antecedent.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Leo tripped, and he dropped the cup. The marked part “Leo” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: Pronoun case changes a pronoun for its job: I or she as subject; me or her as object.
cards.explanation: The form a pronoun takes for its job: subjective (I, she, they), objective (me, her, them) or possessive (my/mine, her/hers, their/theirs).
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: She — waves.; Sam waves — at her..

cards.definition: A verb is a doing or being word, like run, jump or is.
cards.explanation: A word that shows an action, state or experience and can show tense (past or present). Verbs are the head of a clause.
cards.illustrationAlt: A child jumps with both feet off the ground.

cards.definition: An action verb tells what someone or something does.
cards.explanation: A verb that names a physical or mental action (run, throw, think, decide).
cards.illustrationAlt: A child kicks a soccer ball.

cards.definition: A linking verb joins the subject to a word that tells about it, like is in “She is happy.”
cards.explanation: A verb (be, seem, become, appear, feel, look, taste) that links the subject to a subject complement, which renames or describes it, instead of showing an action.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The puppy is sleepy. The marked part “is” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A helping verb helps the main verb, like is in “is running” or has in “has eaten.”
cards.explanation: An auxiliary verb (be, have, do, and the modals) used with a main verb to form tense, aspect, voice, questions and negatives.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: She is running. The marked part “is” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A modal verb like can, may, must or should shows if something is possible, allowed or needed.
cards.explanation: A helping verb (can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would; ought to) that adds meanings such as ability, permission, possibility or obligation. Modals have no -s, -ing or -ed forms and are followed by a base verb.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: You should wear a helmet. The marked part “should” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A transitive verb needs an object to receive the action: “She kicked the ball.”
cards.explanation: A verb that takes at least one object to complete its meaning.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Leo threw the ball. The marked part “threw” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: An intransitive verb makes sense with no object: “The baby slept.”
cards.explanation: A verb that does not need an object to complete its meaning.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The baby slept. The marked part “slept” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A regular verb adds -ed for the past: walk, walked.
cards.explanation: A verb whose past tense and past participle are formed by adding -ed (or -d): play/played, bake/baked.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Yesterday we played. The marked part “played” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: An irregular verb changes in a special way for the past: run becomes ran.
cards.explanation: A verb that does not form its past tense and past participle with -ed (go/went/gone, sit/sat, eat/ate/eaten).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The dog ran home. The marked part “ran” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a little word that makes a new meaning, like give up.
cards.explanation: A verb combined with a particle (adverb or preposition) whose meaning is often different from its parts (give up, look after, turn down).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Please turn down the music. The marked part “turn down” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: An adjective describes a noun: big, red, happy.
cards.explanation: A word that describes or modifies a noun or pronoun, used before a noun (a red ball) or after a verb like be (The ball is red).
cards.illustrationAlt: A large red ball and a smaller blue ball sit side by side.

cards.definition: A comparative compares two things, often with -er or more: taller, more fun.
cards.explanation: The form of an adjective or adverb used to compare two things, made with -er or more (taller, faster, more careful).
cards.illustrationAlt: A giraffe and a shorter zebra stand on the same ground.

cards.definition: A superlative means the most of all, often with -est: tallest, fastest.
cards.explanation: The form of an adjective or adverb that shows the highest degree among three or more, made with -est or most (tallest, most careful).
cards.illustrationAlt: Three trees stand in a row; a star appears above the tallest.

cards.definition: An adverb adds information to a verb, adjective, another adverb or sentence: slowly, very or fortunately.
cards.explanation: A word that modifies a verb, adjective, other adverb or whole clause, often telling how, when, where or how much (quickly, soon, here, very).
cards.illustrationAlt: A turtle walks along a path with footprints behind it.

cards.definition: Where, when and why can start a clause that tells more about a place, time or reason.
cards.explanation: The words where, when and why used to introduce a relative clause about a place, time or reason.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: That is the park where we met. The marked part “where” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A preposition connects a noun or pronoun to other words, showing relationships such as place, time or direction.
cards.explanation: A word that links a following noun, pronoun or noun phrase to the rest of the sentence, often showing place, direction or time (in, on, under, to, after).
cards.illustrationAlt: An orange cat lies under a bed, below the mattress and between the bed legs.

cards.definition: A conjunction is a joining word, like and, but, or because.
cards.explanation: A word that links words, phrases or clauses (and, but, or, so, because, when, although).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: I wanted to swim, but it rained. The marked part “but” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: Coordinating conjunctions (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) join equal parts.
cards.explanation: A conjunction that links words, phrases or independent clauses of equal rank: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so (FANBOYS).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: We ran, and we laughed. The marked part “and” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A subordinating conjunction starts a part that needs the main sentence, like because or when.
cards.explanation: A conjunction (because, when, if, although, after, until, since, while) that introduces a dependent (subordinate) clause and links it to a main clause.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: We stayed in because it rained. The marked part “because” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: Correlative conjunctions come in pairs, like either/or and neither/nor.
cards.explanation: Pairs of conjunctions that work together to join equal parts (either…or, neither…nor, both…and, not only…but also).
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: either; Sam; or; Mia.

cards.definition: An interjection is a word that shows a quick feeling, like wow, oops or hooray.
cards.explanation: A word or short phrase that expresses emotion or reaction and is grammatically separate from the sentence (wow, oops, hey, ouch).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Wow, that is huge! The marked part “Wow” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A determiner comes before a noun to tell which one or how many: the, a, this, my, some.
cards.explanation: A word placed before a noun (and before any adjectives) to specify it as known or unknown, or to show quantity: articles, demonstratives, possessives, quantifiers.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: My dog barked. The marked part “My” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: Articles are the little words a, an and the before a noun.
cards.explanation: The most common determiners: the (definite) and a/an (indefinite).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: An owl hooted. The marked part “An” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: The is a definite article: it points to one special thing we know.
cards.explanation: The word the, used when the speaker and listener know which particular thing is meant.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Pass the cup. The marked part “the” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A and an mean any one, not a special one.
cards.explanation: The words a and an, used for one non-specific thing; an comes before a vowel sound.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: I would like an apple. The marked part “an” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A quantifier tells how much or how many: some, many, few, every.
cards.explanation: A determiner that expresses amount or number (some, many, much, few, every, all, no).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Many birds arrived. The marked part “Many” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: Verb tense is a verb form that helps show time, especially present or past.
cards.explanation: The verb form that shows time. Strictly, English marks two tenses with inflections (present and past); future time is shown with words like will. Schools often teach past, present and future tenses.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: Today — I walk.; Yesterday — I walked..

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: Present tense tells what happens now or what happens all the time.
cards.explanation: The verb form used for now, for habits and general truths, and sometimes for scheduled future events (She walks; The bus leaves at 3).
cards.illustrationAlt: A dog barks at a passing mail carrier; the sentence supplies the tense.

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: Past tense tells what already happened, often with -ed.
cards.explanation: The verb form used for events in the past, usually made with -ed; irregular verbs change in other ways (went, ate).
cards.illustrationAlt: Boot prints lead away from a puddle; the sentence describes an earlier jump.

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: Future-time forms tell about later events: “will walk,” “is going to walk,” or “leaves tomorrow.”
cards.explanation: Ways of talking about future time, most often will + base verb (will walk) or be going to + base verb. The UK glossary notes English has no separate future inflection.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Tomorrow we will visit Grandma. The marked part “will visit” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: Simple tenses are the plain forms: I walk, I walked, I will walk.
cards.explanation: The simple present, simple past and simple future forms, which show time without progressive or perfect aspect.
cards.illustrationAlt: Grouped example: I walk.; I walked.; I will walk..

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: Progressive forms use be and an -ing verb to show something in progress: “She is singing.”
cards.explanation: A verb form made with be + present participle (-ing) that shows an action in progress (I am walking, I was walking, I will be walking).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The baby is sleeping. The marked part “is sleeping” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: Perfect forms use have and a past participle to connect an earlier situation with a later time.
cards.explanation: The perfect uses have, has or had plus a past participle; future perfect uses will have. It connects an earlier event or situation to a reference time. It need not mean finished: “I have lived here for years” can describe a situation continuing now.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: She has finished the drawing. The marked part “has finished” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: Perfect progressive shows something that kept going up to a time: “I have been waiting.”
cards.explanation: A verb form combining perfect and progressive aspect (have/had been + -ing) for an action continuing up to a point in time.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: We have been waiting for an hour. The marked part “have been waiting” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: Aspect shows how we view an event over time, such as in progress or connected to an earlier time.
cards.explanation: Aspect concerns the time structure or viewpoint of a situation, not simply when it occurs. Progressive presents an event in progress; perfect relates an earlier situation to a reference time. Perfect can describe completed events or situations that continue.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: is reading — in progress; has read — earlier ↔ now.

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: The base form is the plain verb with no ending, like jump or eat.
cards.explanation: The simplest form of a verb with no added ending, used after to and after modal verbs and listed in dictionaries (walk, be, eat).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: I can jump. The marked part “jump” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: An infinitive is a base verb used with to, like “to run,” or without to, like “can run.”
cards.explanation: The base form of a verb, often after to (the to-infinitive) or after modal verbs. As a verbal it can act as a noun, adjective or adverb.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: I want to swim. The marked part “to swim” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: The present participle is the -ing form of a verb, like running.
cards.explanation: The -ing form of a verb, used in progressive tenses (is running) or as an adjective (a running tap).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The barking dog woke us. The marked part “barking” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: The past participle is the form used after has or was, like eaten or walked.
cards.explanation: The verb form used in perfect tenses (has eaten) and the passive (was eaten), and as an adjective (a broken toy). Regular ones end in -ed.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: I have eaten. The marked part “eaten” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: A gerund is an -ing verb used as a noun, like swimming in “Swimming is fun.”
cards.explanation: A verbal ending in -ing that functions as a noun: as a subject, object, subject complement or object of a preposition.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Swimming is fun. The marked part “Swimming” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: A verbal is a verb form that does another job, like noun or describing word.
cards.explanation: A word formed from a verb that functions as a noun, adjective or adverb: gerunds, participles and infinitives.
cards.illustrationAlt: Connected diagram: swim; Swimming — is fun.; the swimming — child.

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: A finite verb anchors a clause through tense or mood; it can be a main verb or helper.
cards.explanation: A finite verb carries tense or functions in a finite mood such as an imperative. In “She is running,” is is finite and running is non-finite. A finite verb can be an auxiliary, not just the main lexical verb. Infinitives and participles do not independently mark tense.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: She is running. The marked part “is” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: In active voice, the subject does the action: “The dog chased the ball.”
cards.explanation: The ordinary, non-passive grammatical pattern. With an action verb, the subject typically performs the action: The dog chased the ball. Active clauses can also describe states: She knows the answer. Voice is a grammatical pattern, not a measure of energy.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: The dog; chased; the ball..

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: In passive voice, the subject gets the action: “The ball was chased by the dog.”
cards.explanation: A sentence pattern where the subject receives the action, formed with be (or get) + past participle; the doer may follow by or be left out.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: The ball; was chased; by the dog..

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: A verb’s mood shows if you state, ask, command, or wish something.
cards.explanation: Mood concerns how a clause presents a situation, for example as an ordinary assertion (indicative), a command (imperative), or a demand or imagined situation (subjunctive). Many school resources additionally label interrogative and conditional patterns as moods; other grammars treat these as clause type and conditional constructions. These are alternative frameworks, not five universally agreed English verb inflections.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: The gate is open.; Close the gate.; If I were taller….

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: The indicative mood states facts or asks real questions.
cards.explanation: The verb mood used for ordinary statements and questions about what is or was.
cards.illustrationAlt: Grouped example: The sun rises.; The day begins..

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: The imperative mood gives a command or instruction: “Sit down.”
cards.explanation: The verb mood for commands, requests and instructions, using the base form with an understood subject (you).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Wash your hands. The marked part “Wash” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: An interrogative pattern asks a question, often using a question word or a helper before the subject.
cards.explanation: A question-form clause, such as “Did you finish?” Many grammars call this interrogative clause type rather than a separate verb mood; the verb can be indicative. Some school resources use the label interrogative mood.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: You did finish.; Did you finish?.

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: The conditional mood says what would happen if something else happened.
cards.explanation: A construction expressing a condition and its consequence, often using if and would, could or might. Some school resources call it conditional mood; many grammars analyze it using modal verbs and conditional clauses instead. Not every use of would is conditional.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: If it snowed, we would build a snowman. The marked part “would build” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: Subjunctive forms express demands, suggestions or imagined situations: “I ask that she be ready”; “If I were a bird.”
cards.explanation: A rare, formal verb form for wishes, demands and situations contrary to fact (If I were…, I insist that he be…).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: If I were a dragon, I could fly. The marked part “were” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.category: Verb forms: tense, aspect, voice and mood
cards.definition: A tense shift changes verb tense; it is an error only when the change does not fit the time.
cards.explanation: A change from one verb tense to another within a sentence or text. It is appropriate when time or viewpoint changes; it is an error when it unintentionally disrupts the intended time relationships.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: YESTERDAY; opened; saw.

cards.definition: A word is a unit of language with meaning or a grammatical job; we can say or write it.
cards.explanation: A unit of language with meaning or a grammatical function. Words can be spoken or written; written English normally separates them with spaces. A word can have one letter, such as I or a. Contractions and compounds complicate simple space-based counting.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Cats can jump. The marked part “can” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A sentence expresses a complete message; written sentences normally start with a capital and end with punctuation.
cards.explanation: A group of words grammatically connected to each other but not to words outside it; it typically has a subject and a finite verb, and in writing starts with a capital letter and ends with end punctuation.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: The; dog; digs..

cards.definition: A complete sentence has a who or what and tells what they do or are.
cards.explanation: A complete sentence contains at least one independent clause. A statement normally has a subject and a predicate; a command may have an understood you: “Sit!” Length alone does not determine completeness.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: The bird; sings..

cards.definition: The subject is who or what the sentence is about.
cards.explanation: The noun phrase, pronoun or clause that has the subject role and normally controls verb agreement. It usually precedes the verb in a statement. In an active action clause it is often the doer; in a passive clause it can be the receiver: The ball was kicked.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The puppy barked. The marked part “The puppy” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: The predicate tells what the subject does or is.
cards.explanation: The part of a clause that contains the verb and says something about the subject (everything except the subject).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The puppy barked at the gate. The marked part “barked at the gate” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: The simple subject is the main noun or pronoun in the subject.
cards.explanation: The key noun or pronoun of the subject, without its modifiers.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The tiny brown puppy barked. The marked part “puppy” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: The complete subject is the subject with all its describing words.
cards.explanation: The simple subject plus all the words that modify it.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The tiny brown puppy barked. The marked part “The tiny brown puppy” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: The simple predicate is the main verb, with its helpers.
cards.explanation: The main verb (with any helping verbs) of the predicate.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The puppy was barking loudly. The marked part “was barking” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: The complete predicate is the verb and all the words that go with it.
cards.explanation: The simple predicate plus its objects, complements and modifiers.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The puppy was barking loudly at the door. The marked part “was barking loudly at the door” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: The object is who or what gets the action.
cards.explanation: A noun, pronoun or noun phrase that usually comes after the verb and shows what the verb acts on; it can become the subject of a passive verb.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Mia kicked the ball. The marked part “the ball” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: The direct object gets the action: “She threw the ball.”
cards.explanation: The noun or pronoun that directly receives the action of a transitive verb (answers what? or whom? after the verb).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Leo baked cookies. The marked part “cookies” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: The indirect object is who gets the thing: “She gave me a book.”
cards.explanation: The noun or pronoun that tells to whom or for whom the action is done; it comes between the verb and the direct object.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Leo baked his mom cookies. The marked part “his mom” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A complement finishes the meaning, telling more about the subject or object.
cards.explanation: A word or phrase that completes the meaning of a verb by adding information about its subject (subject complement) or its object (object complement); unlike an object it can be an adjective.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The news made me happy. The marked part “happy” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A subject complement comes after a linking verb and renames or describes the subject.
cards.explanation: A noun, pronoun or adjective after a linking verb that renames (predicate nominative) or describes (predicate adjective) the subject.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: My aunt is a pilot. The marked part “a pilot” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A phrase is a word or group of words that works together as a unit in a sentence.
cards.explanation: A grammatical unit built around a head word, such as a noun phrase or prepositional phrase. For school-level contrast, a non-clausal phrase does not have its own subject–finite-verb structure. A phrase can contain a clause: “the dog that barked.” Some grammars allow one-word phrases.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: We ran across the bridge. The marked part “across the bridge” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A noun phrase is a noun with its helper and describing words: “the big red ball.”
cards.explanation: A grammatical unit with a noun or pronoun as its head, with any determiners and modifiers: the blue butterfly; foxes with bushy tails. It can include a relative clause and, in some grammars, consist of just one word.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The fluffy white cat slept. The marked part “The fluffy white cat” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: An expanded noun phrase adds details to a noun: “the big dog with muddy paws.”
cards.explanation: A noun phrase lengthened with adjectives, nouns or prepositional phrases to describe and specify (the strict maths teacher with curly hair).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The tall teacher with curly hair smiled. The marked part “The tall teacher with curly hair” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A verb phrase is the main verb plus its helping verbs: “will be going.”
cards.explanation: A main verb together with its auxiliaries (and, in some grammars, its objects and modifiers).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: She will be singing tonight. The marked part “will be singing” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A prepositional phrase starts with a word like in or under and ends with a noun: “under the bed.”
cards.explanation: A phrase headed by a preposition followed by a noun, pronoun or noun phrase (its object), often acting as an adjective or adverbial.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The cat slept on the warm rug. The marked part “on the warm rug” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: An adverbial tells when, where, how or why, like “after lunch” or “very slowly.”
cards.explanation: A word, phrase or clause used like an adverb to modify a verb or clause, such as an adverb, preposition phrase, noun phrase or subordinate clause.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: We played outside after lunch. The marked part “after lunch” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A fronted adverbial comes before the main clause: “Later that day, we found the map.”
cards.explanation: An adverbial placed before the main subject and verb of a sentence, usually followed by a comma.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Later that day, we found the map. The marked part “Later that day” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: An appositive is a noun next to another noun that tells who or what it is.
cards.explanation: A noun or noun phrase placed beside another noun to identify or explain it; set off by commas when not essential.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: My dog, a fluffy poodle, loves snow. The marked part “a fluffy poodle” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A participial phrase uses a participle, like laughing or broken, to describe a noun.
cards.explanation: A phrase headed by a present or past participle that acts as an adjective.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Laughing loudly, the kids ran outside. The marked part “Laughing loudly” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: An absolute phrase adds a picture detail to the whole sentence: “Her hair flying, she ran.”
cards.explanation: A phrase made of a noun plus a participle (and modifiers) that modifies a whole clause rather than one word.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Her hair flying in the wind, she raced downhill. The marked part “Her hair flying in the wind” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A clause is built around a verb and usually has a subject: “the bell rang.”
cards.explanation: A group of words built around a verb, usually with a subject. Clauses can be main (independent) or subordinate (dependent).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: When the bell rang, we ran outside. The marked part “When the bell rang” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: An independent clause can stand alone as a sentence.
cards.explanation: A clause with a subject and verb that expresses a complete thought and can be a sentence by itself.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: We ran outside when the bell rang. The marked part “We ran outside” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A dependent clause has a subject and verb but can’t stand alone.
cards.explanation: A clause that does not express a complete thought on its own and depends on a main clause; it often begins with a subordinating conjunction or relative pronoun.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: We ran outside when the bell rang. The marked part “when the bell rang” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A relative clause tells more about a noun, starting with who, which, that or where.
cards.explanation: A subordinate clause that modifies a noun, usually introduced by a relative pronoun or adverb (who, which, that, whose, where, when); the pronoun can sometimes be left out.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The kite that I made is blue. The marked part “that I made” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A noun clause is a whole clause doing a noun’s job.
cards.explanation: A dependent clause that functions as a noun (subject, object or complement), often starting with that, what, whether or how.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: What you said was kind. The marked part “What you said” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: An adverbial clause tells when, why, or if, like “because it rained.”
cards.explanation: A dependent clause that acts as an adverbial, introduced by a subordinating conjunction (when, because, if, although).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Because it rained, we stayed in. The marked part “Because it rained” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A simple sentence has one independent clause and no dependent clauses.
cards.explanation: A sentence with one independent clause and no dependent clauses (the UK glossary calls it a single-clause sentence).
cards.illustrationAlt: Grouped example: The cat naps.; [ one clause ].

cards.definition: A compound sentence joins two or more independent clauses, using a conjunction or a semicolon.
cards.explanation: A sentence with two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (with a comma) or a semicolon.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: I like cats.; and; Sam likes dogs..

cards.definition: A complex sentence has one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.
cards.explanation: A sentence with one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: We stayed in; because; it rained..

cards.definition: A compound-complex sentence has at least two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause.
cards.explanation: A sentence with two or more independent clauses and at least one dependent clause.
cards.illustrationAlt: Grouped example: When it rained,; we stayed in,; and Sam read..

cards.definition: A statement tells something and ends with a period.
cards.explanation: A sentence that states a fact or opinion; it usually ends with a period (full stop).
cards.illustrationAlt: A child calmly points toward a blue sky.

cards.definition: A question asks something and ends with a question mark.
cards.explanation: A sentence that asks for information, usually with a question word or with a helping verb before the subject; it ends with a question mark.
cards.illustrationAlt: A puzzled child searches near an empty coat hook.

cards.definition: A command tells someone to do something: “Close the door.”
cards.explanation: A sentence that gives an order, instruction or request; the subject you is usually understood.
cards.illustrationAlt: A child gestures toward an open door with a cat nearby.

cards.definition: An exclamation shows strong feeling and ends with an exclamation mark.
cards.explanation: A sentence that expresses strong feeling and ends with an exclamation mark. (The UK curriculum defines exclamations narrowly, starting with What or How: What a big cake!)
cards.illustrationAlt: A delighted child opens their arms beside a large birthday cake.

cards.definition: A fragment is part of a sentence pretending to be a whole one.
cards.explanation: A group of words punctuated as a sentence that lacks a subject, a finite verb, or a complete thought (often a dependent clause on its own).
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: Because it rained…; We stayed in — because it rained..

cards.definition: A run-on jams two sentences together with no stop between them.
cards.explanation: Two or more independent clauses joined with no punctuation or conjunction (also called a fused sentence).
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: BEFORE — It rained — we stayed in.; AFTER — It rained. — We stayed in..

cards.definition: A comma splice joins two sentences with only a comma, which isn’t enough.
cards.explanation: An error where two independent clauses are joined by a comma alone; fix with a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: BEFORE — It rained, — we stayed in.; AFTER — It rained; — we stayed in..

cards.definition: The subject and verb must match: “he hops,” “they hop.”
cards.explanation: The rule that a verb matches its subject in number (and person): singular subjects take singular verbs, plural subjects take plural verbs.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: one dog — runs; two dogs — run.

cards.definition: A pronoun must match the noun it stands for: one girl → she; two girls → they.
cards.explanation: A pronoun should refer clearly to its antecedent and fit its number and person. Singular they is standard for a person whose gender is unknown or whose pronouns are they/them: Someone left their coat. They retains forms such as they are.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: the girls; their umbrellas.

cards.definition: A modifier is a word or phrase that tells more about another word.
cards.explanation: A word, phrase or clause that makes another word’s meaning more specific (adjectives modify nouns; adverbs modify verbs).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The sleepy cat yawned. The marked part “sleepy” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A misplaced modifier is in the wrong spot and makes a silly meaning.
cards.explanation: A modifier placed too far from the word it describes, so it seems to describe the wrong word.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: Only Mia — saw a dog.; Mia saw — only a dog..

cards.definition: A dangling modifier describes someone who isn’t even in the sentence.
cards.explanation: An introductory phrase that has no clear word to modify, because the intended doer is missing.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: BEFORE — Walking to school, — the rain began.; AFTER — Walking to school, — I noticed rain..

cards.definition: Parallel structure means listing things in the same pattern: “to run, to jump, to swim.”
cards.explanation: Using the same grammatical form for items in a list or paired ideas.
cards.illustrationAlt: Grouped example: swimming; hiking; biking.

cards.definition: A morpheme is the smallest word part that has meaning, like un-, help or -ful.
cards.explanation: The smallest unit of language that carries meaning; a word can be one morpheme (cat) or several (un + help + ful).
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: un; help; ful.

cards.definition: Morphology is how words are built from parts.
cards.explanation: The study of a word’s internal make-up: root words, prefixes, suffixes and other changes (mouse → mice).
cards.illustrationAlt: Connected diagram: word building; unhelpful — un + help + ful; dogs — dog + s.

cards.definition: A root word is the main part of a word that other parts are added to.
cards.explanation: The core word to which prefixes and suffixes are added (help in helpful, unhelpful, helping). In the UK school sense it can stand alone; in Greek/Latin roots it may not.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: replay The marked part “play” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A base word is a whole word you can add parts to, like jump in jumping.
cards.explanation: A complete word that can stand alone and to which affixes are added (jump → jumped, jumping, jumper).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: jumping The marked part “jump” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: Many English words have Greek or Latin roots, like graph (write) or aud (hear).
cards.explanation: A word part from Greek or Latin that carries core meaning and appears in many English words (graph = write, photo = light, aud = hear).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: autograph The marked part “graph” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A prefix is a word part added to the front that changes the meaning, like un- or re-.
cards.explanation: A morpheme added to the beginning of a word to make a new word (un-, re-, pre-, dis-, mis-).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: unhappy The marked part “un” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A suffix is a word part added to the end, like -ful, -less or -ly.
cards.explanation: A morpheme added to the end of a word to form a new word or a new form (-ful, -less, -ness, -er, -ly, -ed, -s). Suffixes cannot stand alone.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: helpful The marked part “ful” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: An affix is any word part added to a word: a prefix or a suffix.
cards.explanation: A morpheme attached to a word or root to change its meaning or form; prefixes and suffixes are affixes.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: disagree The marked part “dis” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: An inflection changes a word’s form for grammar, like -s for more or -ed for past.
cards.explanation: A change in a word’s form that marks grammar such as plural, tense or comparison (dog → dogs, walk → walked, good → better) without making a new word.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: looked The marked part “ed” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: Derivation is making a new word from another word, like teach → teacher.
cards.explanation: Forming a new word, often of a different word class, by adding affixes (teach → teacher, happy → happiness).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: teacher The marked part “er” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A compound word is two words put together to make a new one, like sunflower.
cards.explanation: A word made of two or more root words (bookshelf, ice-cream, notebook), written closed, hyphenated or open.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: sun; + flower; = sunflower.

cards.definition: A contraction squeezes two words into one, using an apostrophe: do not → don’t.
cards.explanation: A shortened word formed from two words, with an apostrophe showing the missing letters (I’m, can’t, we’ll).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: I can’t find it. The marked part “can’t” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A syllable is a beat in a word. Clap it: but-ter-fly has three.
cards.explanation: A unit of pronunciation usually organized around a vowel sound: cat has one syllable; butterfly has three. In some accents a consonant can form the syllable nucleus, as in the last syllable of button. Clapping spoken beats is a useful starting point.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: but; ter; fly.

cards.definition: A word family is a group of words built from the same word, like help, helper, helpful.
cards.explanation: Words related by shared morphology and meaning (teach, teacher; solve, solution, dissolve). In early phonics the term also means rhyming groups (cat, hat, bat).
cards.illustrationAlt: Connected diagram: help; helper; helpful; unhelpful.

cards.definition: Etymology is the history of a word: where it came from.
cards.explanation: A word’s origin and history, including earlier forms in English or other languages and how its meaning has changed.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: earlier language; word history; word today.

cards.definition: A synonym is a word that means the same or almost the same, like big and large.
cards.explanation: A word or phrase with the same or nearly the same meaning as another (talk/speak, old/elderly).
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: big; large.

cards.definition: An antonym means the opposite, like hot and cold.
cards.explanation: A word with the opposite meaning of another (hot/cold, light/dark).
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: hot; cold.

cards.definition: Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings, like hear and here.
cards.explanation: Words pronounced alike but different in meaning and usually spelling (to/too/two, there/their/they’re).
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: hear — listen; here — this place.

cards.definition: Homographs are spelled the same but mean different things, and may sound different: a bow and to bow.
cards.explanation: Words spelled alike but different in meaning or origin, and sometimes in pronunciation (lead the metal / to lead; bow of a ship / bow and arrow).
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: bow — a ribbon knot; bow — bend forward.

cards.definition: Homonyms are words that look and sound the same but mean different things, like bat and bat.
cards.explanation: In the UK school glossary: two different words that are spelled and pronounced the same (bark of a dog / bark of a tree). Merriam-Webster notes the word is also used loosely for homophones and homographs.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: bat — flying animal; bat — sports tool.

cards.definition: A multiple-meaning word has more than one meaning, like duck (a bird) and duck (bend down).
cards.explanation: A word with two or more meanings; context shows which meaning is used (duck the bird / to duck).
cards.illustrationAlt: A duck swims on the left; a child ducks beneath a low branch on the right.

cards.definition: Context clues are the words around a new word that help you guess its meaning.
cards.explanation: Information in the surrounding sentence or passage (definitions, examples, restatements, contrasts) that helps a reader figure out a word’s meaning.
cards.illustrationAlt: Connected diagram: The bat flew — out of the cave.; flew; cave.

cards.definition: Shades of meaning are small differences between similar words, like warm, hot and boiling.
cards.explanation: Fine distinctions in strength or manner among related words (look, peek, glance, stare; large, gigantic).
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: annoyed; angry; furious.

cards.definition: Connotation is the feeling a word gives, like “cozy” feels nicer than “small.”
cards.explanation: The feelings or associations a word suggests beyond its dictionary meaning.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: thrifty — positive feeling; stingy — negative feeling.

cards.definition: Denotation is a word’s plain dictionary meaning.
cards.explanation: The literal, dictionary definition of a word, without the feelings or associations it may carry.
cards.illustrationAlt: Grouped example: home; the place — where someone lives.

cards.definition: An analogy explains something by comparing relationships or showing how it is like something more familiar.
cards.explanation: A comparison showing that the relationship between one pair of things is like the relationship between another pair; also an extended comparison used to explain.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: bird → nest; bee → hive.

cards.definition: A letter is one symbol of the alphabet, like a, b or c.
cards.explanation: One of the 26 symbols of the English alphabet, written as capital (uppercase) or small (lowercase).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: cat The marked part “c” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A vowel is a speech sound made with open airflow; a, e, i, o, u and sometimes y represent vowels.
cards.explanation: A speech sound made with an open mouth and no blocking of air; in writing, a, e, i, o, u and sometimes y represent vowels.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: cat The marked part “a” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A consonant is a speech sound made by blocking or narrowing airflow; letters such as b and t represent consonants.
cards.explanation: A speech sound made by blocking or narrowing the air with lips, tongue or teeth; most alphabet letters stand for consonants.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: big The marked part “b” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A short vowel is a vowel sound like a in cat, e in bed or i in sit.
cards.explanation: The vowel sounds heard in words like cat, bed, sit, hot, cup.
cards.illustrationAlt: Grouped example: cat; map; short a.

cards.definition: A long vowel says its own name, like a in cake or i in kite.
cards.explanation: Vowel sounds that match the letter names, often spelled with final -e or vowel teams (cake, kite, boat).
cards.illustrationAlt: Grouped example: A; cake; long a.

cards.definition: A blend is two or three consonants side by side where you hear each sound, like bl or str.
cards.explanation: A group of adjacent consonants in which each sound is still heard (bl, st, tr, str).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: block The marked part “bl” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A digraph is two letters that make one sound, like sh, ch or th.
cards.explanation: A grapheme of two letters representing one phoneme (sh in ship, ee in feet); a split digraph has a letter between (a–e in cake).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: ship The marked part “sh” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A phoneme is one small sound in a word. Cat has three: /k/ /a/ /t/.
cards.explanation: The smallest unit of sound that can change a word’s meaning (tap vs. cap). English has about 44, depending on accent.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: /sh/; /i/; /p/.

cards.definition: A grapheme is the letter or letters that write one sound, like ph for /f/.
cards.explanation: A letter or group of letters that represents one phoneme (t, sh, igh, ph).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: dolphin The marked part “ph” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A silent letter is written but not said, like k in knee.
cards.explanation: A letter in a word’s spelling that is not pronounced (k in knight, b in lamb, w in write).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: knee The marked part “k” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A sight word is any word you recognize instantly without sounding it out each time.
cards.explanation: A sight word is a written word an individual reader recognizes automatically. A high-frequency word occurs often in print. The categories overlap but are not identical: any familiar word can become a sight word. Connect spelling to sounds rather than teaching children to guess from shape.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: a written word; instant recognition.

cards.definition: Punctuation marks are signs like . , ? ! that help readers read sentences the right way.
cards.explanation: Conventional marks and features of writing other than spelling (. , ; : ? ! - – ( ) “ ” ’, plus capitals, spaces and paragraph breaks) that show sentence boundaries and meaning.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Are you ready? The marked part “?” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A period is the dot that ends a statement.
cards.explanation: The mark (.) used at the end of a statement or mild command, and after some abbreviations; called a full stop in British English.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: I like pizza. The marked part “.” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A question mark (?) goes at the end of a question.
cards.explanation: The mark (?) that ends a direct question.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Do you like pizza? The marked part “?” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: An exclamation mark (!) shows strong feeling, like surprise or excitement.
cards.explanation: The mark (!) used after an exclamation, a strong command or an interjection to show strong feeling.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: We won! The marked part “!” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A comma separates items or parts of a sentence and helps make the meaning clear.
cards.explanation: A mark (,) that separates items in a series, joins independent clauses with a coordinating conjunction, sets off introductory elements and nonessential information, and is used in dates, addresses and dialogue.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: It rained, so we stayed in. The marked part “,” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: An apostrophe (’) shows missing letters (can’t) or who owns something (Sam’s).
cards.explanation: A mark (’) with two main jobs: showing where letters are missing in a contraction (I’m) and marking possession (Hannah’s mother, the girls’ coats).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: can’t The marked part “’” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: Quotation marks (“ ”) go around the exact words someone says.
cards.explanation: Marks (“ ” or ‘ ’) placed around direct speech or quoted words; also used for some titles. British English calls them inverted commas or speech marks.
cards.illustrationAlt: Grouped example: Mia said,; “I am ready.”.

cards.definition: A colon (:) introduces a list or explanation: “Bring three things: a hat, a coat and gloves.”
cards.explanation: A mark (:) used to introduce a list, a quotation or an explanation, or to mark a boundary between independent clauses.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Bring these: a hat and a coat. The marked part “:” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A semicolon (;) joins two closely related sentences without and or but.
cards.explanation: A mark (;) that links closely related independent clauses, or separates items in a complex list.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: It rained; we stayed in. The marked part “;” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A hyphen (-) is a short line that joins words, like well-known or twenty-one.
cards.explanation: A short mark (-) that joins words into compounds (one-way street, forty-six) or attaches some prefixes; it can prevent ambiguity (man-eating shark).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: well-known The marked part “-” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A dash (—) is a long line that adds an extra thought or a dramatic pause.
cards.explanation: A long mark (— or –) used to set off extra information, show a break in thought or mark a boundary between clauses.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: I opened it—it was empty! The marked part “—” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: Parentheses ( ) hold extra information that the sentence could do without.
cards.explanation: Curved marks ( ) around added information or an aside; the sentence must still make sense without it. British English often calls them brackets.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: My cousin (the tall one) plays drums. The marked part “(the tall one)” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: An ellipsis (…) is three dots that show words left out or a trailing pause.
cards.explanation: Three dots (…) that show an omission from a quotation or a pause or unfinished thought. (In grammar, ellipsis also means leaving out expected words.)
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: I wonder… The marked part “…” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: Capital letters start sentences and names, and the word I is always a capital.
cards.explanation: Use of uppercase letters for the first word of a sentence, the pronoun I, proper nouns, titles, dates and holidays.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The dog sleeps. The marked part “T” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: Bullet points are dots that start each item in a list.
cards.explanation: Symbols (•) that mark separate items in a vertical list; punctuate them consistently.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: • hat The marked part “•” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: Literal language means exactly what the words say.
cards.explanation: Words used in their ordinary, exact dictionary meaning.
cards.illustrationAlt: Grouped example: Rain is falling.; water from clouds.

cards.definition: Figurative language uses words in a fun, not-exact way to make a picture in your mind.
cards.explanation: Language that goes beyond literal meaning to create effect, using figures of speech such as simile, metaphor, personification, hyperbole and idiom.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: “cats and dogs”; heavy rain.

cards.definition: A simile compares two things using like or as: “as fast as a cheetah.”
cards.explanation: A figure of speech that compares two unlike things using like or as.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Mia ran as fast as a cheetah. The marked part “as fast as a cheetah” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A metaphor says one thing is another to compare them: “The classroom was a zoo.”
cards.explanation: A figure of speech that understands one thing in terms of another without an explicit like/as comparison. It may state an identity (“The classroom was a zoo”) or imply it (“A wave of worry washed over her”).
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: the classroom; “a zoo”.

cards.definition: Personification gives human actions or feelings to things that aren’t people.
cards.explanation: A figure of speech that gives human qualities, actions or feelings to animals, objects or ideas.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The wind whispered through the trees. The marked part “wind whispered” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: Hyperbole is a huge exaggeration: “I’m so hungry I could eat a horse!”
cards.explanation: Deliberate, extreme exaggeration for emphasis or humor, not meant to be taken literally.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: I have a million chores tonight. The marked part “a million” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: An idiom is a saying that means something different from its words, like “break a leg.”
cards.explanation: A fixed group of words whose meaning is different from the meanings of the individual words.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: “Break a leg!”; Good luck!.

cards.definition: A proverb is a short, well-known saying that gives advice, like “Look before you leap.”
cards.explanation: A short traditional saying that expresses a general truth or piece of advice.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: Look; before; you leap..

cards.definition: Alliteration is when nearby words start with the same sound: “Silly snakes slide.”
cards.explanation: The repetition of the same sound, usually consonants, at the beginning of nearby words.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: Silly; snakes; slide..

cards.definition: Onomatopoeia is a word that sounds like the noise it names, like buzz or splash.
cards.explanation: The use of words whose sound imitates the sound they describe (buzz, sizzle, crash).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: The bee went buzz. The marked part “buzz” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: Imagery is describing words that help you see, hear, smell, taste or feel something.
cards.explanation: Vivid descriptive language that appeals to the senses and creates pictures in the reader’s mind.
cards.illustrationAlt: Connected diagram: dry leaves; crackle; smoky smell.

cards.definition: Words rhyme when their ending sounds match, like cat and hat.
cards.explanation: The repetition of the same ending sounds in words, often at the ends of lines of poetry.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: c + at; h + at.

cards.definition: Rhythm is the beat you hear in a poem or song.
cards.explanation: The pattern of stressed and unstressed beats in language, especially in poetry.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: TAP; tap; TAP; tap.

cards.definition: Repetition is saying a word or line again to make it stand out.
cards.explanation: Repeating a word, phrase or line for emphasis, rhythm or cohesion.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: Run,; run,; run!.

cards.definition: A symbol is a thing in a story that stands for a bigger idea, like a dove for peace.
cards.explanation: The use of an object, character or element to represent another idea; symbols often recur in a text.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: repaired locket; renewed trust.

cards.definition: Irony is when what happens or what is said is the opposite of what you expect.
cards.explanation: A contrast between what is expected and what actually happens (situational), what is said and what is meant (verbal), or what a character knows and what the reader knows (dramatic).
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: fire station — protects from fire; fire station — burns down.

cards.definition: Verbal irony is saying the opposite of what you mean, like “Great weather!” in a storm.
cards.explanation: Saying something that means the opposite of the literal words, often for humor.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: a soaking storm; “Lovely weather!”.

cards.definition: Dramatic irony is when the reader knows something a character doesn’t.
cards.explanation: Irony created when the audience or reader knows something important that a character does not, creating suspense or humor.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: reader knows — party inside; Sam wonders — what is inside.

cards.definition: Foreshadowing is a hint early in a story about what will happen later.
cards.explanation: The use of details, description and mood early in a work that hint at later events.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: early: — bridge creaks; later: — bridge collapses.

cards.definition: A flashback jumps back in time to show something that happened earlier.
cards.explanation: A scene that interrupts the present action of a story to show earlier events.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: story now; years earlier; story now.

cards.definition: Mood is the feeling a story gives you, like spooky or cheerful.
cards.explanation: The atmosphere or emotional feeling a text creates for the reader through setting, imagery and word choice.
cards.illustrationAlt: Connected diagram: empty dark house; echoing steps; uneasy feeling.

cards.definition: Tone is the writer’s attitude, like serious, funny or angry.
cards.explanation: The writer’s or speaker’s attitude toward the subject or audience, shown through word choice and style.
cards.illustrationAlt: Grouped example: “Ugh…”; “Another rainy day.”.

cards.definition: A theme is an important message or insight a story explores, not always a lesson or moral.
cards.explanation: The central message, lesson or insight about life that a story, poem or drama conveys; in early grades often called the moral or central message.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: small kindness; friendship; connection.

cards.definition: An allusion is a quick mention of a famous story or person to add meaning.
cards.explanation: An indirect reference to a well-known person, place, event or work (myth, literature, history).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Moving the boulder was a Herculean task. The marked part “Herculean” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A pun is a joke that plays with a word’s two meanings or sounds.
cards.explanation: A play on words that uses multiple meanings or similar sounds for humor.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: math problems — exercises; life problems — troubles.

cards.definition: An oxymoron puts two opposite words together, like “jumbo shrimp.”
cards.explanation: A figure of speech that combines contradictory terms (deafening silence, jumbo shrimp).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: A deafening silence filled the room. The marked part “deafening silence” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A euphemism is a gentle way to say something hard or rude.
cards.explanation: A mild or indirect word or phrase used in place of one that may seem harsh or unpleasant.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: Our hamster passed away. The marked part “passed away” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A paradox is a statement that seems impossible but has a true point.
cards.explanation: A statement or idea that seems self-contradictory but reveals a truth.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: less clutter; more clarity.

cards.definition: A stanza is a group of lines in a poem, like a paragraph in a story.
cards.explanation: A group of lines forming a unit in a poem, separated from other stanzas by a space.
cards.illustrationAlt: Grouped example: line one — line two; line three — line four.

cards.definition: A paragraph is a group of sentences about one idea.
cards.explanation: A section of writing organized as a unit, normally developing a main idea and beginning on a new line. A paragraph can be one sentence. In fiction, a new paragraph may mark a change of speaker, action, place or time.
cards.illustrationAlt: Connected diagram: dogs love games; fetch a ball; find a toy.

cards.definition: The topic is what a piece of writing is about, in a word or two.
cards.explanation: The subject of a text or paragraph, usually named in a word or short phrase (e.g., “sharks”).
cards.illustrationAlt: Connected diagram: FROGS; food; habitat; growth.

cards.definition: A topic sentence tells what the whole paragraph will be about.
cards.explanation: A sentence, often at the start, that states the main idea of a paragraph.
cards.illustrationAlt: Grouped example: Dogs help people.; guiding; rescuing.

cards.definition: Supporting details are facts or examples that back up the main idea.
cards.explanation: Specific facts, examples, reasons or descriptions that explain or prove the main idea of a paragraph.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: help people — stay safe; guide around — obstacles.

cards.definition: A concluding sentence wraps up the paragraph.
cards.explanation: A final sentence that restates or sums up the main idea and gives a sense of closure.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: guiding + rescuing; dogs help — keep people safe.

cards.definition: The main idea is the most important point the writer is making.
cards.explanation: The central point of a paragraph or text, supported by key details.
cards.illustrationAlt: Connected diagram: ways to save water; fix drips; close taps; collect rain.

cards.definition: A key detail is an important bit of information in a story or text.
cards.explanation: An important piece of information that helps a reader understand a story or support the main idea.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: lost puppy; seen at the park; search the park.

cards.definition: Transitions are linking words like first, next, also and because that connect ideas.
cards.explanation: Words and phrases (first, then, however, for example, in addition) that connect ideas, sentences and paragraphs and show their relationships.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: First mix the flour. Next add water. The marked part “Next” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: Cohesion means all the sentences stick together and make sense as a whole.
cards.explanation: The quality of a text whose parts clearly connect, helped by cohesive devices such as pronouns, determiners, conjunctions, adverbials and repetition.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: Joe got a bike.; He loved it..

cards.definition: A thesis states the central point an essay develops and supports; it can take more than one sentence.
cards.explanation: A statement, usually in the introduction, that gives the central claim or main point that an essay will develop and support.
cards.illustrationAlt: Connected diagram: a school garden; science lessons; shared work.

cards.definition: A claim is what you say is true and will try to prove.
cards.explanation: A statement or position that a writer argues for and supports with reasons and evidence.
cards.illustrationAlt: Grouped example: Our school should; add shaded seating..

cards.definition: A counterclaim is the other side’s argument that a writer answers.
cards.explanation: An opposing claim that a writer acknowledges and responds to in an argument.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: more recess — more play; more recess — less lesson time?.

cards.definition: Evidence is information, examples or quotations that support a point; stronger evidence comes from reliable sources.
cards.explanation: Facts, data, examples or quotations that support a claim or reason.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: dated counts; check the method; support a claim.

cards.definition: A reason tells why you think something.
cards.explanation: A statement explaining why a writer holds an opinion or claim; reasons are supported by facts and details.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: I like summer because I can swim. The marked part “because I can swim” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: A fact is something that can be proven true.
cards.explanation: A statement that can be checked and shown to be true.
cards.illustrationAlt: Grouped example: triangle; 3 sides.

cards.definition: An opinion is what someone thinks or feels; others may disagree.
cards.explanation: A personal belief, judgment or preference. Preferences cannot be settled like factual measurements, but opinions can contain factual claims that should be checked and can be supported or challenged with evidence.
cards.illustrationAlt: Grouped example: “Pizza is the best!”; personal preference.

cards.definition: The introduction is the beginning that tells readers what the writing is about.
cards.explanation: The opening part of a text that introduces the topic or situation and, in essays, often states the thesis or opinion.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: opening question; topic; what comes next.

cards.definition: The conclusion is the ending that wraps up the writing.
cards.explanation: The closing part of a text that sums up, restates or reflects on the main point and gives a sense of closure.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: important points; bring together; ending.

cards.definition: Narrative writing tells a story, real or made up.
cards.explanation: Writing that recounts real or imagined experiences or events in a sequence, with characters, setting and details.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: Leo hears a knock; opens the door; finds a surprise.

cards.definition: Informative writing teaches facts about a topic.
cards.explanation: Writing that examines a topic and conveys information and ideas clearly, using facts, definitions and details.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: seed takes water; root grows; shoot appears.

cards.definition: Opinion writing tells what you think and gives reasons why.
cards.explanation: Writing that states an opinion on a topic or text and supports it with reasons (in grades K–5).
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: I enjoy drawing; because; I invent creatures.

cards.definition: Argument writing uses reasons and evidence to convince readers a claim is right.
cards.explanation: Writing that supports claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence, often acknowledging counterclaims (grades 6–12).
cards.illustrationAlt: Connected diagram: plant shade trees; temperature data; reasons.

cards.definition: Point of view is who is telling the story and how they see it.
cards.explanation: The perspective from which a story is told (first, second or third person), and more broadly a character’s or narrator’s outlook.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: I opened the gate.; She opened the gate..

cards.definition: First person tells the story using I and we.
cards.explanation: Narration by a character in the story, using I, me, we.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: I opened the gate. The marked part “I” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: Second person talks right to the reader using you.
cards.explanation: Narration or writing that addresses the reader directly as you (common in instructions and choose-your-path stories).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: You open the door and see a dragon. The marked part “You” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: Third person tells the story about others using he, she and they.
cards.explanation: Narration by someone outside the story, using he, she, they; it can be limited to one character or all-knowing (omniscient).
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: She ran to the bus. The marked part “She” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: The narrator is the voice telling the story.
cards.explanation: The character or voice that tells the story to the reader.
cards.illustrationAlt: Grouped example: “I am Pip the cat.”; “Here is my story…”.

cards.definition: A character is a person, animal or other being who takes part in a story.
cards.explanation: A person, animal or being who takes part in the events of a story.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: brave mouse; trapped lion.

cards.definition: The main character is who the story is mostly about.
cards.explanation: The central character of a story, who usually faces the main conflict (the protagonist).
cards.illustrationAlt: Connected diagram: LEO; his choices; his search; his discovery.

cards.definition: The setting is where and when a story happens.
cards.explanation: The time and place in which the events of a story take place.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: WHERE — mountains; WHEN — snowy night.

cards.definition: The plot is what happens in a story from beginning to end.
cards.explanation: The sequence of events in a story, usually built around a conflict that rises to a climax and is resolved.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: dog is lost; Leo searches; dog is found.

cards.definition: The conflict is the problem the characters must solve.
cards.explanation: The main struggle or problem in a story, between characters, between a character and nature or society, or within a character.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: children want out; water blocks exit.

cards.definition: The climax is a major turning point where a story’s main conflict reaches its greatest tension.
cards.explanation: The turning point of a story, where tension peaks and the conflict is faced.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: tension builds; decisive rescue; tension eases.

cards.definition: The resolution shows how a story’s conflict ends or what remains after it; not every problem is solved.
cards.explanation: The part of a narrative that shows the outcome of the main conflict, often following the climax. It may settle loose ends, show consequences or leave questions unresolved. An ending need not be happy or solve every problem.
