cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: friends disagree; decide to share; fly kite together.

cards.definition: Sequence is the order things happen: first, next, then, last.
cards.explanation: The order in which events or steps occur, often signaled by time words (first, then, finally).
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: 1 — whole egg; 2 — egg cracks; 3 — chick emerges.

cards.definition: Dialogue is the words characters say to each other in a story.
cards.explanation: Conversation between characters, written with quotation marks and speaker tags.
cards.illustrationAlt: Example: “Are you coming?” asked Mia. The marked part “Are you coming?” is repeated in a connected tile.

cards.definition: Sensory details tell how things look, sound, smell, taste or feel.
cards.explanation: Descriptive details that appeal to the five senses to make writing vivid.
cards.illustrationAlt: Connected diagram: fresh bread; crackle; sweet smell.

cards.definition: A summary tells the most important parts in a short way, using your own words.
cards.explanation: A brief restatement of the main ideas and key details of a text, in the reader’s own words, without personal opinion.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: many story details; important events; short account.

cards.definition: To retell is to tell a story again in order, with the important parts.
cards.explanation: To recount a story’s events in sequence, including key details.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: egg cracks; chick emerges; chick walks.

cards.definition: A draft is a version of your writing that you can develop and change.
cards.explanation: An early version of a piece of writing, written to get ideas down before revising and editing.
cards.illustrationAlt: Grouped example: version 1; still developing.

cards.definition: To revise is to make your writing better by adding, cutting or moving ideas.
cards.explanation: To reconsider and change the content and organization of writing to improve meaning and clarity.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: old ending; clearer ending.

cards.definition: To edit is to fix spelling, capitals and punctuation mistakes.
cards.explanation: Editing improves correctness and consistency in grammar, spelling, capitalization, punctuation and style. Proofreading is a final check for remaining surface errors, often after layout. Revision usually focuses more on ideas, organization and meaning; these activities can overlap.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: teh; the.

cards.definition: To publish is to share your finished writing with others.
cards.explanation: To produce a final, polished version of writing and share it with an audience.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: finished story; class book; readers.

cards.definition: Your audience is the people who will read or hear your writing.
cards.explanation: The intended readers or listeners of a piece; writers adjust words and style to suit them.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: instructions; first-grade readers.

cards.definition: Purpose is why you are writing: to tell a story, to teach, or to convince.
cards.explanation: The reason for writing, such as to entertain, inform, explain or persuade.
cards.illustrationAlt: Sequence: letter + reasons; request a swing.

cards.definition: Voice is how your writing sounds like you: your own style and personality.
cards.explanation: The distinctive style and personality of a writer or narrator, created by word choice, sentence style and tone.
cards.illustrationAlt: Grouped example: “Whoa.”; “Best. Day. Ever.”.

cards.definition: Formal language is for serious times; informal language is for friends.
cards.explanation: A variety of language suited to a situation: formal (presentations, essays) vs. informal (chat with friends), shown by vocabulary and grammar choices.
cards.illustrationAlt: Comparison: “Hey, can I…?”; “I would like — to request…”.

cards.definition: A heading is a title for a section that tells what it’s about.
cards.explanation: A title at the start of a section of text that helps readers find and preview information.
cards.illustrationAlt: Grouped example: What Frogs Eat; insects; other small prey.
